description: The Lectio Edition of the Dhammapada: the Buddha's verses in plain current English, with its terms, its opening, and its review record.
what: About four hundred short verses, sayings of the Buddha gathered by theme. It is the best loved and most quoted book in Buddhism. The verses were made to be learned by heart.
why: F. Max Müller's translation of 1881 was made for the Sacred Books of the East. It is a scholar's version in Victorian prose. It says "tabernacle" for a house and "sin" for harm, and it explains terms in parentheses in the middle of a verse.
Some of it is simply wrong. Müller has "All forms are unreal" where the Pali says all things are without a self.
The Lectio Edition gives the twenty-six chapters in plain English that keeps the weight of a saying. It follows the Pali where Müller departs from it. Müller stays in the app beside it.
choices_lede: The review set these rules and swept the whole work for each.
choices: Nothing in a verse explains the verse. "Nirvana" appears only where the Pali has the word. Müller's parenthetical glosses, which the draft had written into the lines, were removed.
Where Müller is wrong, the edition follows the Pali. Brahma the god is not "Brahman".
Each Pali term has one English word. *Appamada* is "heedfulness" and its opposite is "heedlessness". The Buddha's *dhamma* is "the teaching". The *sangha* is "the Order". A *bhikkhu* is a monk.
"Evil" or "harm", not "sin". The Pali word carries no guilt before a god.
The verses keep Müller's numbering, so the two can be compared.

divergences.older: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought" (Müller)
divergences.lectio: the mind is chief of all
divergences.why: Müller's opening is loved and it interprets. The edition keeps his cadence as the first line, then gives the Pali's three claims in order: the mind goes first, the mind is chief, things are made of mind. The draft had said the mind "makes" everything. The Pali does not, and the review took it out.

divergences.lectio: Hatred ends only by love—this is the ancient and unchanging law.
divergences.why: The Pali word means timeless, a law that has always held. "An old rule" is too small for it.
The chapter turns on this one word. It means unbroken watchfulness. "Earnestness" sounds like sincerity.
By tradition these are the Buddha's words on awakening. The Pali image is a house: builder, rafters, ridgepole. "Tabernacle" brings in a Biblical word the Pali does not have.

divergences.older: "Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord?" (Müller)
divergences.lectio: You are your own master; who else could be?
divergences.why: The Pali speaks to the listener. Müller makes it an abstract remark about the self.

divergences.older: "Not to commit any sin, to do good" (Müller)
divergences.lectio: Not to do any evil; to cultivate good; to purify one's own mind
divergences.why: The verse Buddhists call the summary of the teaching. "Sin" imports guilt before a god.

divergences.lectio: All things are without a self
divergences.why: These are the three marks of existence: impermanent, suffering, without a self. Müller's third is a mistranslation, and the edition corrects it.

checked: Müller (1881). The Pali is not in the bundle, so readings of the Pali came from the reviewing model's own knowledge of the text.
open: The editor's own read of all twenty-six chapters.
The edition's overview still speaks of "the mind that makes the world". That sits a little against the correction to verses 1 and 2.
Verse 128, which was missing, has been restored. The provenance should say so.
Müller's text in the bundle runs verses 127 and 128 together. That is a fault in how his edition was brought in, to be fixed there.
